presentingComplaint: Found drowsy with right-sided weakness and word-finding difficulty by her daughter, evolving over roughly one hour.
history: Frail 84-year-old woman living with her daughter, baseline Clinical Frailty Score 6 (mobilises with a frame). Background of longstanding hypertension and permanent atrial fibrillation for which she takes apixaban 5 mg BD. Previous lacunar TIA 3 years ago. Two prior episodes of transient visual disturbance in the past year (possibly amyloid spells) not investigated. This morning she complained of a mild 'pressure' headache and mild nausea, then over the next hour became progressively drowsy with difficulty getting her words out and a weak right arm. No preceding trauma or fall witnessed. No fever, no neck stiffness. Last apixaban dose taken this morning.
examination: Elderly frail woman, drowsy but rousable to voice, GCS E3V4M6 (13). Non-fluent (expressive) dysphasia. Right hemiparesis MRC 3/5 in arm, 4/5 in leg, with a right facial droop. Right plantar upgoing. No neck stiffness, no papilloedema. Irregularly irregular pulse. No external head injury. No focal source of infection.
imaging: Non-contrast CT head: acute 4.3 x 3.1 cm lobar haematoma in the left temporoparietal region with mild surrounding oedema and 3 mm midline shift; no intraventricular extension, no subdural or extradural collection. Lobar location with adjacent cortical superficial siderosis suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy rather than deep hypertensive haemorrhage. CT angiogram: no 'spot sign', no macrovascular cause (aneurysm/AVM).
differentialDiagnoses: Acute ischaemic stroke (cardioembolic, given AF) — excluded by CT showing haemorrhage
Chronic/acute subdural haematoma in a frail anticoagulated elder — excluded on CT
Underlying brain tumour with haemorrhage — no mass/enhancement on imaging
Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage — no SAH, no aneurysm on CTA
finalDiagnosis: Spontaneous lobar intracerebral haemorrhage in an anticoagulated frail elderly patient, most consistent with cerebral amyloid angiopathy.
citations: AHA/ASA — Guideline for the Management of Patients With Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage — 2022
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Cerebrovascular Diseases (Hemorrhagic Stroke / Intracerebral Hemorrhage)
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective. Priority is rapid anticoagulation reversal (andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC for apixaban), controlled BP lowering (target SBP ~140), and neurosurgical/stroke consult.
contraindications: Do not give antiplatelet/anticoagulant agents acutely
Avoid abrupt/excessive BP reduction below ~130 mmHg SBP given cerebral autoregulation in the elderly
Avoid thrombolysis — this is haemorrhage, not ischaemic stroke
edgeCases: Near-normal INR does not exclude clinically significant DOAC effect — anti-Xa/apixaban level confirms recent activity and reversal is still indicated
Lobar location + superficial siderosis in an elder points to amyloid angiopathy and high re-bleed risk, influencing decisions on restarting anticoagulation
Mild headache and gradual drowsiness (not thunderclap) is a realistic atypical elderly presentation and can be mistaken for ischaemic stroke or delirium
expectedMaiK: Elderly anticoagulated patient with acute focal deficit and reduced GCS — obtain urgent non-contrast CT head; a lobar haematoma diagnoses spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, mandating immediate DOAC reversal and controlled BP management.
expectedNextQuestions: Exact time of last apixaban dose and indication for anticoagulation?
Any witnessed trauma or fall (to exclude traumatic haemorrhage/subdural)?
Baseline functional status/frailty and prior neurological events?
Current blood pressure trend and airway/GCS trajectory?
